flashcards.q: What is LangSmith's self-hosting posture, and roughly what does it cost?
flashcards.a: Closed source; self-hosting is Enterprise-only, requiring a sales conversation and a reported minimum contract north of $100K, with no self-serve self-host path.

flashcards.q: What license is Langfuse's core under, and what happened to Langfuse in January 2026?
flashcards.a: MIT-licensed core (tracing, evals, prompt management, datasets, playground, no usage limits self-hosted). Acquired by ClickHouse on 16 January 2026, with both companies publicly committing to keep it MIT-licensed and self-hostable.

flashcards.q: What license does Arize Phoenix use, and why does that matter for procurement?
flashcards.a: Elastic License 2.0 -- source-available but NOT OSI-approved open source. Some procurement policies require OSI-approved licenses specifically, which blocks Phoenix even though it's free and fully-featured to self-host.

flashcards.q: What license does Laminar use, and how OTel-native is it?
flashcards.a: Apache 2.0 (true OSI-approved open source). Natively ingests raw OpenTelemetry with no translation/adapter layer required.

flashcards.q: Roughly how does LangSmith's cost compare to Langfuse's at 1M trace events/month?
flashcards.a: LangSmith ~$2,514/month vs Langfuse Cloud ~$101/month -- over a 20x gap at the same volume.

flashcards.q: Rank the four platforms (LangSmith, Langfuse, Phoenix, Laminar) from most to least OTel-native.
flashcards.a: Laminar (raw OTel, no translation) > Phoenix (OTel + OpenInference conventions) > Langfuse (OTel is one of several SDK integrations) > LangSmith (LangGraph-native first, OTel secondary).

flashcards.q: How does Laminar's pricing model differ from a typical per-trace or per-span model, and why does it favor agent workloads?
flashcards.a: Laminar bills on compressed data volume, compressing agent traces roughly 20x before storage -- this favors chatty multi-step agents (a typical run emits 40-75 spans) since most of that text data compresses well.

flashcards.q: What infrastructure does self-hosting LangSmith require beyond the enterprise license, roughly?
flashcards.a: A minimum ~16+ vCPU / 64+ GB RAM Kubernetes cluster plus managed Postgres/Redis/ClickHouse, landing around $950-1,150/month in raw infra cost for a small deployment.

flashcards.q: Name a real risk with Langfuse's ClickHouse acquisition commitment, and the historical pattern that motivates the caution.
flashcards.a: License commitments made during an acquisition's press cycle have a documented history of quietly reversing 12-18 months later once attention fades (cited precedents: MySQL, Redis, Elastic) -- the current MIT commitment is real but not a permanent guarantee.

flashcards.q: When is LangSmith usually the wrong choice?
flashcards.a: When you're not already deep in LangChain/LangGraph, need cheap/fast self-hosting without a six-figure enterprise contract, or are cost-sensitive at real production trace volume.

flashcards.q: When is Phoenix usually the wrong choice?
flashcards.a: When procurement requires an OSI-approved license specifically (Elastic License 2.0 doesn't qualify), or when the team wants a polished dashboard-first SaaS experience rather than Phoenix's notebook-first, Jupyter-flavored workflow.

flashcards.q: What is the practical test for whether your instrumentation is locked into a specific observability platform?
flashcards.a: Instrument with raw OTel + the GenAI semantic conventions, then try swapping only the exporter endpoint between two backends (e.g. Phoenix and Laminar) with zero code changes -- if that works, you're not locked in; if it requires SDK-specific rewrites (as with LangSmith/Langfuse for full feature parity), you are.

flashcards.q: What specific tooling does LangSmith offer that a generic OTel-native platform doesn't, and why might a team still choose it despite cost/lock-in?
flashcards.a: Node-by-node LangGraph state diffs and 'replay against a new model' regression isolation, plus a first-party Prompt Hub with zero assembly -- genuinely deeper for teams fully committed to LangChain/LangGraph as their agent runtime.

flashcards.q: Why is comparing these four platforms on a feature checklist alone misleading?
flashcards.a: All four now claim tracing, evals, prompt management, and datasets, so a checklist shows near-parity; the real differentiators (license, self-hosting cost/accessibility, cost curve at 10-100x pilot volume, migration cost to leave) only surface when modeled against your actual growth and constraints.

flashcards.q: Why should you re-verify pricing/licensing figures for these platforms before using them in a real procurement decision?
flashcards.a: This market re-prices and re-licenses every few months; every figure in this comparison is dated 2026-08-01 and has a short shelf life.
